status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading; not a gate action)
dataset_family: Clinica Universidad de Navarra Memory Unit (Pamplona, Spain), retrospective real-world clinical aMCI cohort, Oct 2013 to Mar 2021; non-ADNI
method_family: Classical biomarker-stratified survival analysis: visually read binary amyloid-PET (A+/A-) and FDG-PET (N+/N-) status, per-test sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV, Kaplan-Meier with log-rank and hazard ratios. No fusion model, no machine learning, no discrimination metric (AUC, C-index or accuracy) for the combined profile.
what_it_shows: 145 aMCI patients (133 with FDG-PET; 116 with complete follow-up, 75 converters / 41 non-converters) were cross-classified by visual amyloid-PET and FDG-PET reads into A+/N+ (54), A+/N- (34), A-/N+ (4) and A-/N- (40). Table 3 gives sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for each PET test ALONE at 12-48 months; no accuracy figures are given for the combined profile. The only combined-biomarker result is a Kaplan-Meier comparison inside the amyloid-positive subgroup: A+/N+ converted earlier than A+/N- (log-rank chi2 = 4.16, p = 0.0415). So adding the FDG-PET read to amyloid-PET status splits amyloid-positive patients into earlier and later converters. That is incremental prognostic stratification of time to conversion over amyloid-PET alone. It is not a head-to-head test of prediction performance.
why:
IDENTITY: the PDF (Eur J Nucl Med Mol Imaging 2025;52:3567-3577, doi 10.1007/s00259-025-07275-2; Echeveste, Prieto, Guillen, Jimenez, Montoya, Villino, Riverol, Arbizu) matches the summaries.md block 'Paper 578' in title and author list (block line ~50016). The map entry is marked 'formula-unverified', but the title and authors on page 1 match. Read in full from page 1 to the References (page 9) and the page 9 back matter (limitations, conclusion, declarations).

STATED FORM ('auxiliary-data-aware fusion improves progressive-MCI prediction over unimodal baselines in head-to-head tests'): NO. (1) There is no fusion model of any kind. The 'combination' is a 2x2 cross-tabulation of two visual reads. (2) Neither input is auxiliary, metadata or side-information. Both are co-primary imaging biomarkers (a second PET tracer). (3) There is no head-to-head comparison of prediction performance. Table 3 reports accuracy only for each test alone, and no sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC, C-index or model-fit comparison is given for the combined profile against amyloid-PET or FDG-PET alone. (4) The combination is never compared with FDG-PET alone, and there is no non-imaging baseline. Nothing of the stated form survives.

NARROWED FORM ('adding auxiliary information to an imaging model ... improved progressive-MCI prediction over the same imaging model alone'): PARTLY. What it shows: adding the FDG-PET read to amyloid-PET status separates amyloid-positive aMCI into faster and slower converters (A+/N+ vs A+/N-, log-rank chi2 = 4.16, p = 0.0415, p.6). That is incremental prognostic information on time to conversion over the amyloid read alone, within the study. What it does not show: (a) any improvement in prediction of who progresses, since no discrimination or accuracy figure exists for the combination; (b) an improvement over the whole cohort, since the test is confined to the A+ subgroup (n = 88); (c) auxiliary information in the narrowed record's sense. The added input is a second primary imaging modality, not source-task attention, side-information used inside an imaging model, age or cognitive scores. Round 1 treated a second primary brain modality (MEG in P-488) as not auxiliary; on that precedent the fit is weaker still. (d) The 'imaging model' is a binary visual read, not a model.

SOURCE DEFECTS AND RISKS: (i) The results print the A+/N+ median as '27.80 [CI 2.70-20.40]', a CI that excludes its own point estimate. The abstract and discussion give '27.79 [CI 20.40-33.21]' and call it a mean in the discussion (p.8), so the summary statistic and its CI cannot be pinned down from the source. (ii) The methods say 'All analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education level' (p.4), but the only combined result is a log-rank chi-square, which is unadjusted, and no adjusted HR for A+/N+ vs A+/N- is printed. (iii) Patients who converted to a non-AD dementia were counted as 'lost' (p.4, Fig. 1 caption), i.e. censored, an informative-censoring and competing-risk issue. 29 of 145 (20%) were lost. (iv) PET was 'part of the routine diagnostic process' (p.2). The PET readers were blinded to clinical data, but the paper does not state that the neurologists who judged conversion to 'dementia due to AD' were blinded to the PET results, so incorporation bias cannot be ruled out from the source. (v) The group sizes sum to 132 against 133 with FDG-PET. (vi) The authors list the limits themselves: clinical rather than research setting, no control group, unequal groups, variable follow-up, no post-mortem confirmation (p.9).

INDEPENDENCE: non-ADNI (a Navarra clinical cohort), so on a narrowed partly it could not lift the family count in any case, since only a yes counts. It shares no sample, recruitment site or author with the current supporters (P-3, P-104, P-81, all ADNI) or with any round-1 candidate (P-43 Innsbruck; P-554 SMS/Huashan; P-488 BioFIND; the rest ADNI). Outside the VF-15 set, P-1164 comes from the same Clinica Universidad de Navarra memory clinic (a different SCD cohort, 2001-2017) and shares authors Villino, Montoya, Jimenez and Riverol. It is not a VF-15 supporter or candidate. Published peer-reviewed open-access article; not a preprint. Registry row (Dataset 'In-house clinical cohort - Clinica Universidad de Navarra', Best_Metric '... (no AUC)') is consistent with the PDF.

quotes.quote: The patients were classified into four groups based on whether Amyloid-PET (A) and FDG-PET (N) were positive (+) or negative (-). The patients were then clinically followed to establish progression to dementia due to AD.
Taking both tests together, the time to conversion was faster in A+/N + versus A+/N- patients (27.79 [CI 20.40–33.21] vs. 37.38 [CI 20.73–48.26] months).
Using both biomarkers during the initial diagnosis enhances the prediction of short-term conversion.
After the clinical diagnosis, all patients underwent amyloid deposition PET scanning as part of the routine diagnostic process, and 133 patients additionally had an FDG-PET scan.
All analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education level, with significance set at P < 0.05.

The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value were obtained for each test over 4 years. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated to estimate the probability of conversion over time based on the biomarker results.
On follow-up, 75 out of 116 patients progressed to dementia due to AD, while 29 patients were lost (i.e. lost to follow-up or converted to a different type of dementia).

markedly steeper decline compared to the amyloid-negative group (hazard ratio [HR]: 5.007 [95% CI: 2.521–9.942]; p < 0.0001) (Fig. 3). ... steeper decline versus FDG-negative patients (HR: 3.127 [95% CI: 1.82–5.36]; p < 0.001) (Fig. 3).

Combining both PET scan findings, A+/N + patients converted significantly earlier than A+/N- patients (median: 27.80 [CI 2.70–20.40] vs. 37.38 (CI 20.73–48.26) months; chi2 = 4.16, p = 0.0415) (Fig. 4).
In our cohort, A+/N + patients progressed earlier and to a greater extent versus A+/N- patients (mean: 27.79 [CI 20.40–33.21] vs. 37.38 [CI 20.73–48.26] months).

The data in this study was drawn from a clinical setting, which can differ from those acquired from a research setting. Additionally, there was no control group, and the number of patients in each group was unequal. Furthermore, the clinical follow-up period in the present study varied between patients, which could be considered a limitation especially among those that did not exhibit progression. Lastly, the aetiological diagnosis was determined based on the patients' clinical progression during the follow-up period without a postmortem confirmation of the diagnosis.
